title: Contrastive Learning for User Sequence Representation in Personalized Product Search

problem.claim: Personalized product search methods need accurate and robust user representations to generate personalized search results.

gap.claim: Existing methods struggle because real-world search logs can be sparse or noisy.

contributions.claim: A contrastive learning framework, CoPPS, is proposed to learn high-quality user representations for personalized product search.
Three data augmentation and contrastive learning strategies construct self-supervision signals from original search behaviours.
The contrastive learning tasks use an external knowledge graph and correlations within and between user sequences to discover meaningful search patterns.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on public Amazon datasets are reported to verify the effectiveness of the approach.

narrative_sequence.summary: Personalization in product search is receiving increasing attention.
Existing methods use historical search logs to model individual user search interests.
Sparse or noisy search logs make accurate and robust user representation learning difficult.
CoPPS addresses the issue with contrastive learning, data augmentation, self-supervision, an external knowledge graph, and correlations among user sequences.
The authors report effectiveness on public Amazon datasets.

source_observation.claim: Self-supervision can be constructed from augmented user search behaviours and sequence correlations.

interpretation.claim: When labeled personalization data are limited or noisy, structured behavioral transformations and relational signals may support representation learning.

application.claim: Consider contrastive objectives that combine behavior augmentation, within-sequence relations, between-sequence relations, and external knowledge.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which augmentation or relational signal is necessary, nor whether the approach generalizes beyond the reported Amazon datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the three augmentation strategies.
The abstract does not report dataset sizes, baselines, metrics, or numerical results.
The abstract does not establish independent verification or generalization beyond the public Amazon datasets.
